Back when the Greece joined the Euro they had to meet deficit levels. This they did by lying. Unfortunately in 2010 the real figures came out.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_government-debt_crisis#Debt_levels_revealed_.282010.29

Now to realise why this is bad you have to realise why Greek politicians were so keen on the Euro in the first place. Since the reintroduction of democracy in 1974 Greece has run rather large deficits

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_government-debt_crisis#Unsustainable_and_accelerating_debt-to-GDP_ratios

What's going on is that Greek politicians borrowed money to pay off various special interests, and in turn those special interests voted for them. The Euro made this a bit easier because at that point all countries in the Euro were seen as being more or less the same risk. So that Greece could borrow at near German rates instead of the rates they had with the Drachma. Still joining the Euro (2001) didn't make things much worse.

However once the 2008 crisis hit unemployment rose everywhere, debt to GDP rose too. So long as the figures were successfully falsified all was OK but in 2010 the real figures came out. At which point people wouldn't buy Greek government bonds unless the government pushed up those bonds interest rates, but the Greek government couldn't afford to pay the new higher rates on ~175% of GDP and couldn't print money as they would have done if they used the Drachma. So they needed a bailout.

Now the terms of the bailout were that Greece reduce its deficit to sustainable levels. That requires spending cuts which are obviously very unpopular. So the current Syriza government opposes those.

There's an alternative of course. Greece could default on its debt. They'd probably have to leave the Euro too. Syriza has been trying to get a debt write off that would enable them to stay inside the Euro but the the Germans who contribute most of the cash to the EU realise if they do this then so will Spain, Italy, Portugal etc.

Right now banks are closed and they may well be planning on a default and exit from the Euro. However if they do that the new currency will be sharply devalued - previously markets had estimated by up to 80%. This means that anyone who has savings will lose most of them. On the upside outside the Eurozone they'd at least have control of their currency and can inflate their way out of debt and austerity.

Greek banks are closed this week to prevent everyone withdrawing their money at once.

Greece will miss a debt payment of $1.73 billion to the international monetary fund on June 30th.

Greece will hold a national referendum Sunday, July 5th to vote whether to accept the bailout conditions proposed by the European Union (EU), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the European Central Bank (ECB)
